episodes.171338: An easterly wave that had been in place over southern New Mexico and Arizona all week finally tracked over New Mexico on August 20, 2022. As it did so, it brought an above normal amount of precipitation as precipitable water amounts rose to near record values. This brought widespread, beneficial rainfall to most of northern and central New Mexico with the highest 24-hour rainfall totals of two to four inches across areas south of Interstate 40 where the easterly wave tracked. The system did lack a sufficient amount of instability, and thus, stratiform rain was most common with embedded thunderstorms. These light rainfall rates meant that the traditional summertime flash flooding was not the main threat. Rather, rises on rivers, creeks, and streams were with the long duration event. Flooding was reported in Mesa along U.S. Highway 285 which stranded motorists. The McBride burn scar also experienced flooding thanks to hours of steady rainfall. Across Chaves County, the Pecos River experienced record flooding with major impacts felt for several days near Roswell, Hagerman, Dexter, and Lake Arthur.
episodes.171361: A squall line produced localized wind damage during the late morning hours over a small portion of central Virginia.
episodes.171394: Deep moisture and light winds led to conditions favorable for morning waterspouts. Warm and moist conditions in advance of an arriving mid level trough of low pressure, nose of an upper level jet, and inland moving sea breeze circulation, favored an environment conducive for severe thunderstorms during afternoon hours.
episodes.171395: Warm and moist conditions in advance of an arriving mid level trough of low pressure, nose of an upper level jet, and inland moving sea breeze circulation, favored an environment conducive for severe thunderstorms during afternoon hours.
episodes.171529: A moisture-rich monsoon fetch, infused by tropical moisture from a wave that moved off the Gulf of Mexico and through South Texas, brought significant amounts of moisture into West Texas. The approach of an upper level storm system well to our north and northwest caused the fetch of monsoon moisture to bend squarely over West Texas. In addition to embedded disturbances within the monsoon, a couple of weak frontal boundaries moved southward into the region. Working together, the moisture, mid-level disturbances, and low-level boundaries generated widespread showers and thunderstorms. The increasingly tropical airmass led to very efficient rain rates and locally heavy rainfall through the evening and overnight hours from the 20th into the 21st.
episodes.171600: A midlevel Pacific low pressure system undercut the area of high pressure over the Great Basin as it dropped into the Northern Rockies. Monsoon moisture increased across the region with precipitable water values ranging from 125 to 175% of normal across the Four Corners. Clearing conditions the morning of the 20th led to increased instability over southeast Utah which led to some stronger thunderstorms during the late evening hours. The anomalously high moisture values across the area resulted in heavy rain with thunderstorms. Additionally, winds aloft supported the training of thunderstorms. This heavy rainfall led to widespread flash flooding and debris flows across portions of Grand and San Juan counties.
episodes.171607: Isolated thunderstorms occurred in a moist and unstable air mass ahead of a slow-moving cold front. The front extended from Lake Michigan southwest to the Ozark Plateau of southwest Missouri when a storm produced isolated tree damage in southern Illinois.
episodes.171759: An isolated thunderstorm developed across the western slopes of the northern Green Mountains in a moderately unstable airmass and moved north into Enosburg Falls where a brief and localized microburst downed a few trees.
episodes.171786: Showers and thunderstorms developed near a boundary over central Virginia. Anomalous moisture was present, and the storm motion was slow which led to areas of flooding and flash flooding.
episodes.171858: A waterspout was observed over southern Lake Michigan during the late morning of August 21st, several miles offshore of Diversity Harbor in Chicago.
episodes.171886: Afternoon sea breeze thunderstorms produce gusty winds over the coastal waters around Tampa Bay.
episodes.171889: Afternoon thunderstorms produce wind damage near Ellenton in Manatee County.
episodes.172076: Pre-frontal storms developed in eastern Ohio on the afternoon of August 21st. Broken cloud coverage in the warm sector enhanced MLCAPE to 1500J/kg; effective shear was modest at 25-30kt. However, it was enough to produce quarter-size hail in discrete cells.
episodes.172183: A tropical wave moved across the area, increasing convergence at the lower levels. Later in the period, low level moisture was provided by the proximity of a surface trough. Additionally, an upper level low approached from the northeast, providing instability aloft, as high pressure at all level weakened.
episodes.172231: A surface low drifted east-southeastward from far-east-central Iowa into northwestern Illinois during the evening of the 20th through wee hours of the 21st. This allowed the accompanying warm front to drift northeastward across the Middle Ohio Valley. Well-ahead of the surface warm front, isolated multicell showers and thunderstorms impacted northwest PA during the late evening of the 20th in an environment that exhibited weak to moderate MUCAPE, moderate DCAPE, and moderate effective bulk shear. One of these thunderstorms generated damaging wind gusts in Edinboro.
episodes.172232: A surface low moved east-southeastward from eastern Iowa to northwestern Ohio during the early afternoon of the 20th through early evening of the 21st. This allowed the accompanying warm front to move northeastward from the Middle Ohio Valley toward the southern shore of Lake Erie. As the front approached Lake Erie, isolated to scattered showers and thunderstorms produced gale-force to storm-force peak wind gusts along the southern lakeshore during the late afternoon and early evening hours of both days. These showers and storms occurred in an environment comprised of moderate MUCAPE, DCAPE, and effective bulk shear, respectively.
episodes.172374: A low pressure system and attendant cold front worked its way through the Ohio Valley on August 21st and into West Virginia. An abundance of moisture was already in place ahead of the frontal passage, which allowed for showers and storms ahead of the front to dump heavy downpours across northeastern West Virginia. Strong to severe storms progressed east of the Ohio River by the afternoon of  the 21st, resulting in a few downed trees in Jackson County and Nicholas County. The threat then transitioned over to flash flooding as heavy downpours prevailed. Localized high water issues arose on roadways in the state that evening into the early morning hours of August 22nd, with one instance of a bridge washing out.
episodes.172378: Discrete cells followed by a well organized line of storms crossed through eastern Ohio during the evening of August 20th before weakening just before midnight in West Virginia and Pennsylvania. Radar suggests the development of a rear inflow jet of 50kts at ten thousand feet as the well-defined line progressed through eastern Muskingum County.
episodes.172390: During the afternoon hours on August 21st, a mid-level trough and associated surface cold front entered central Kentucky from the northwest. Ahead of the surface front, scattered showers and thunderstorms developed, with most storms remaining sub-severe. Overall, instability was relatively modest, with between 1000 and 1500 J/kg mixed-layer CAPE across southern and central Kentucky. Environmental shear was also modest, leading to mainly single cell and multicell clusters of thunderstorms. Nevertheless, a strong cell over Russell County was able to intensify enough to produce isolated wind damage across portions of the county.
episodes.172394: A cold front progressed through Ohio on the afternoon of August 20th and was the primary focus for shower and thunderstorm development. Several areas had tree damage occur in Perry County as a result of strong wind gusts from passing thunderstorms. An afternoon slew of showers and storms developed the next day, once again resulting in a downed tree in Perry County. Heavy downpours and heavily severed soil conditions from previous rainfall led to an instance of flash flooding along State Route 669 near the town of Crooksville.
episodes.172521: An area of low pressure was over New Mexico and helped to bring lift and monsoonal moisture into Southeast New Mexico and West Texas. Along with abundant moisture and lift, instability was also in place. These conditions lead to rain and thunderstorms which moved over the same areas resulting in flash flooding.
episodes.172522: Weak frontal boundary was over central Georgia as a high pressure ridge axis moved northward over the area. Light southwesterly flow allowed for the Atlantic coast sea breeze to push further inland with the boundary merging with the Gulf coast sea breeze between Highway 301 and I-75. Moist airmass (PWATs > 2 in.), ample instability and sea breeze boundary collision led to a severe storm developing in Alachua county. This storm knocked a tree down across the road near Alachua.
episodes.172523: A shortwave trough aloft moved through the region bringing an influx of moisture and lift. Southwest steering flow pinned the Atlantic coast sea breeze to the I-95 corridor. The Gulf coast sea breeze pushed inland developing strong thunderstorms that produced gusts of 40-50 mph in Alachua county. The Gulf sea breeze eventually collided with the Atlantic sea breeze in the late afternoon hours. There was the potential for a wet downburst potential due to cooler mid level temps (-8 deg C at 500 mb) and drier mid level air in the 700-500 mb layer. A severe storm developed over Duval county when the sea boundaries collided. This storm produced downburst winds that uprooted and snapped multiple trees causing damage to a car and fence in the Mandarin area. The storm also produced lots of pea size hail.
episodes.172713: Thunderstorms developed into northwestern Arkansas during the evening of the 20th and continued through the early morning hours of the 21st, as a cold front moved into the area. An isolated thunderstorm briefly became severe, producing damaging winds in Washington County.
episodes.172876: Numerous slow-moving thunderstorms developed in a moist and unstable air mass ahead of a slow-moving cold front. The front extended from Lake Michigan southwest to the Ozark Plateau of southwest Missouri. Locally heavy rain under these storms caused flash flooding of roads.
episodes.172928: A weak distrubance moved through Central New York, triggering scattered thunderstorms. Warm and humid conditions were enough for the environment to become unstable to support a severe thunderstorm in Onondaga County.
episodes.173020: A slow moving thunderstorm brought flash flooding to a small portion of Fulton County on the afternoon of August 21st.  Several roads reported high water and debris.||In Cambria County, road flooding occurred in East Taylor, Summerhill, and Middle Taylor. East Taylor and Middle Taylor townships declared local disaster declarations. Damage was to paved and unpaved roadways, streambeds, and vegetative areas.
episodes.173063: Scattered thunderstorms developed in a warm and humid airmass during the afternoon hours.
episodes.173072: Showers and thunderstorms developed ahead of a low pressure system moving through the Ohio Valley.
episodes.173130: Showers and thunderstorms developed ahead of a low pressure system moving through the Ohio Valley.
episodes.173202: Brief funnel clouds were observed near Beardsley, associated with a thundershower that moved to the southwest across west central Minnesota.
episodes.173215: Heavy rain produced some flash flooding during the late afternoon.
episodes.173226: A thunderstorm produced a funnel cloud near the ICW.
episodes.173331: A large upper trough shifted southeast into the Four State Region on August 21st, along the backside of an upper level low pressure system over the Great Lakes. This trough slowed as it entered the region, and interacted with rich Gulf moisture and available heating to help focus scattered to numerous showers and thunderstorms across the area. Given the weak steering currents aloft, these thunderstorms were slow moving and were very efficient rainfall producers, which resulted in flash flooding across the cities of Longview and Gladewater in East Texas, where widespread rainfall amounts of three to five inches fell.
episodes.173332: A warm front, drifting northward from the Carolinas across the lower Mid-Atlantic, triggered scattered thunderstorms with heavy rain.  Strong heating during the afternoon supported surface-based CAPE values rising into the 2,000 to 2,500 J/Kg range, while precipitable water values ranged from around 1.5 inches along the Blue Ridge to in excess of 1.8 inches across the central Piedmont of Virginia and North Carolina.  Wind speeds through 700 mb were generally around 10 knots, supporting slow cell movement that would contribute to prolonged heavy rainfall over some locations. Many of the storms produced rainfall at 3 to 5 inch per hour rates, which resulted in flash flooding of small streams in the local area.
episodes.173421: Strong to severe storms impacted the eastern half of the Missouri Ozarks during the afternoon and early evening hours, as a slow moving cold front interacted with a destabilizing air mass. Vertical wind shear was sufficient enough for several strong to severe storms to develop from Springfield eastward toward Rolla and Salem.
episodes.173595: A weak mid level disturbance interacted with a moist and unstable air mass over the Sandhills and Coastal Plain and allowed for the development of strong to severe thunderstorms, some of which produced damaging wind gusts.
episodes.173606: A nearby upper low and building instability resulted in isolated severe storms during the afternoon across the eastern Lake Ontario region.
episodes.173668: A complex of showers and thunderstorms moved across the western Carolinas during the early morning hours. A couple of strong cells developed within the complex, with hail reported in Rutherford County, NC.
episodes.173685: Several days of heavy rain continued across southwest New Mexico as a slow moving mid and upper level trough helped produce widespread rain across the region with nearly 5 inches of rain reported near White Sands. As a result of the heavy rain, numerous reports of flash flooding were received.
episodes.173751: Showers and thunderstorms moved west across southeast Arizona from early morning into the evening. Heavy rain produced flooding in parts of the Tucson area as well as parts of Cochise and Santa Cruz counties.
episodes.173803: Persistent moist monsoonal flow fueled thunderstorms over northwest Arizona. Several storms produced flash flooding and severe weather.
episodes.173835: Isolated showers and thunderstorms initially began across parts of southern Gila County, along with eastern Maricopa County and northeast Pinal County, producing locally heavy rainfall leading to isolated flash flooding. By the late afternoon and early evening hours on the 20th, new thunderstorms initiated over the high terrain of northern Arizona. High instability (MUCAPE 2,000-2,500 J/kg) aided in maintaining strong to severe thunderstorms into the Phoenix area as thunderstorms pushed toward the south and into the lower deserts during the evening. DCAPE around 1,000-1,200 J/kg promoted strong to severe downbursts with the strongest thunderstorms. Meanwhile, PWATs around 1.7-1.9 aided in thunderstorms being heavy rainfall producers, leading to several reports of flash flooding. No injuries were reported.
episodes.173842: Flash flooding in several national parks and severe hail were observed with scattered thunderstorms.
episodes.173860: Thunderstorms brought gusty winds and flash flooding to portions of Garfield County.
episodes.173885: A cold front moved through the region. Showers and storms associated with it produced a few reports of damaging winds and large hail.
episodes.173886: A cold front moved through the region. Showers and storms associated with it produced a few reports of damaging winds and large hail.
episodes.173988: Weak surface low pressure slowly moved across northwest Ohio over the southern shore of Lake Erie in north central Ohio during the afternoon and evening hours of August 21st. A warm front was oriented from west to east across the area just south of the lakeshore, while a trailing cold front slowly advanced eastward behind the low. In the warm sector, MUCAPE values of 1000-1500 j/kg, weak deep layer shear, and precipitable water values of 1.6 to 1.7 inches allowed for deep moist convection to develop with heavy rainfall. Upwind propagation vectors were generally out of the southwest at 10 kts or less, promoting slow storm movement with enhanced training potential. Several clusters of storms trained over urban areas in north central Ohio causing localized urban flash flooding as rainfall rates as high as 4 to 5 inches per hour tracked over residential areas.
episodes.173992: Deep monsoon moisture over northern Arizona and a trough of low pressure passing through Utah made for a rather active day across the area.  Thunderstorms produce heavy rain, high winds, and small hail.
episodes.174063: Very heavy rainfall occurred over Webb and Duval Counties associated with a tropical low pressure system on the 15th and 16th. Flood wave that originated in San Casamiro Creek in Webb County flowed into the Nueces River, Major river flooding occurred from southeast La Salle County through McMullen County to Live Oak County from the 17th through the 24th.
episodes.178910: Scattered thunderstorms developed around portions of Mississippi on August 21st. Some became severe and produced damaging wind gusts.

A long duration rain event caused the Pecos River in Chaves County to swell and cause major flooding around the river. Once the Acme gauge to the northeast of Roswell crested to major flood stage, that water slowly traveled south for several days, causing flooding in the Dexter, Hagerman, and Lake Arthur areas. The gauge at Lake Arthur crested to a maximum of 13.37 feet at about 6:45 PM MDT on August 26th. Despite this being well below action stage, major impacts were still felt for several days across southern Chaves County along the Pecos River. During the early morning hours of the 21st, a vehicle attempting to cross a flooded low water crossing was carried about a half mile downstream along Cherokee Road near Hagerman. A water rescue was conducted for the driver who was found sitting on the top of their partially submerged vehicle. Along River Road at Bottomless Lakes, four people had to be rescued. Two of these individuals were rescued from a trapped vehicle while the other two were rescued from the home after they previously chose not to evacuate. Finally, near Dexter, three people had to be rescued from their vehicle. This water rescue proved to be particularly difficult as the flood waters at this point were too high which prevented emergency officials from reaching the stranded travelers. Officials had to drive around Dexter and approach the location from the east to rescue the three individuals. Despite all this, there were no known injuries and damages are a rough estimate.
Rincon Road at Hassayampa River (normally dry) was close due to flooding.  The stream gauge on Martinez Wash at Whickenburg showed a 2 foot rise to 700 CFS rise on this normally dry wash.
Three homes were struck by lightning near the intersection of Legacy Lake Way and Warren Lake Road.

A FCDMC streamflow gage along Sols Wash exceeded alarm stage, making a low water crossing along Vulture Mine Road impassable. At 0424MST, the gage peaked at a depth of 3.65 feet and a flow of 3,822 CFS. A social media video showed Sols Wash flowing across Vulture Mine Road and Wickenburg dispatch reported the road was closed as a result of the flooding. No damage or injuries were reported.

A personal weather station (Weather Underground: KVADUGSP7) recorded a 24-hour rainfall total of 4.84 inches, most of which fell between 2 pm and 9 pm on the 21st.  Rainfall rates were observed at 2 to 3 inches per hour at times during the event.  This total was about a 50-year rainfall event at the 6-hour duration per NOAA Atlas 14 Point Precipitation Frequency estimates.

A personal weather station (Weather Underground: KVAHILLS48) recorded a 24-hour rainfall total of 4.97 inches, which fell between 3 pm and 9 pm on the 21st.  Rainfall rates were observed at 2 to 3 inches per hour at times during the event.  This total was about a 100-year rainfall event at the 6-hour duration per NOAA Atlas 14 Point Precipitation Frequency estimates.

A personal weather station (Weather Underground: KVALEXIN46) recorded a 3-hour rainfall total of 3.94 inches. Rainfall rates peaked at nearly 3 inches per hour during the storm. This total was about a 200-year rainfall event at the 3-hour duration per NOAA Atlas 14 Point Precipitation Frequency estimates.

A personal weather station (Weather Underground: KVAFAIRF60) recorded a 3-hour rainfall total of 3.33 inches, most of which fell between 8 am and 10 am EST on the 21st. Rainfall rates were observed in excess of 3 inches per hour during the event. This total was about a 50-year rainfall event at the 3-hour duration per NOAA Atlas 14 Point Precipitation Frequency estimates.

A long duration rain event across the area caused the Pecos River to swell to record values. The Acme gauge, located to the northeast of Roswell along the river, entered action stage during the early morning hours of August 21st, and water levels continued to rise quickly to a crest of 17.37 feet by about 2 PM MDT. This was well over the major flood stage of 16 feet, and it set a new record for the Acme gauge. The gauge stayed in major flood stage for about seven hours before gradually falling below action stage during the evening hours of August 22nd. This record flooding along the Pecos River caused major impacts in the area. Near Bitter Lake National Wildlife Refuge, the Chaves County emergency manager relayed reports of a truck that was stuck within the flood waters with the driver having to be rescued. Damages are estimated.

Widespread flash flooding across the southern portion of Elyria. Local officials reported that police and fire responded to over 80 residences that were experiencing basement flooding. One housing complex experienced first floor flooding. The majority of the reports came from the Eastern Heights and southern portion of Elyria near the east and west branches of the Black River. Dozens of vehicles became stranded in high water. Most roadways across the southern portion of Elyria has 1 to 3 feet of standing water on them, making them impassable. A gas station awning collapsed from the weight of the water at 9th and Middle Avenue. A swath of 1.5 to 2.5 inches fell in a 30 to 90 minute period across the southern portion of Elyria based on radar estimates. Rainfall rates of 4 to 5 inches per hour immediately preceded the flash flooding, with a peak 30 minute rainfall during this time achieving a 50 year recurrence interval. Storm total rainfall amounts of 3.5 to 4.5 inches were recorded.
High water was observed along State Route 669 nears Crooksville.

A tree was uprooted, fell and damaged a fence of a house near Julington Creek Rd and Micanopy Ln. Time was estimated by radar. Multiple reports of pea size hail were reported in the Mandarin area. A tornado and severe thunderstorm warning were in effect.
Flash flooding was reported in Cannonville and Henrieville, with mud and debris on state Route 12 between the towns.

An approximately 4.5 mile swath of intermittent wind damage, mainly to trees, was surveyed. In the Oakwood area, damage was broad and sporadic in nature, centered on Forrer Boulevard but extending several blocks north and south of the boulevard, over a half mile wide at times. Tree damage in this area was mostly comprised of small and large limb breaks, but a few uprooted trees were noted. Tree damage was not determined to be convergent or to have a particularly strong cross-path component when taken in sum, and pointed more to being non-tornadic in nature.||Gaps of more consistent wind damage were evident before another area of more concentrated wind damage in Kettering along Aragon Avenue and Vale Drive, including an apartment complex which had several trees heavily damaged. Like with the Oakwood area damage, little evidence of a concentrated tornadic circulation existed in the tree damage, which again consisted of large broken limbs and a couple uprooted trees.
A few trees had broken limbs and a house had siding removed from the top of the home and thrown downwind.
